artboards.title: C — Ceiling and what is locked

annotations.text:
A + B + C — the mix

A gives the two tier ceilings (what you can get now, what one tier up is worth). B gives access to the top band. C's headroom is folded in as a sentence rather than a €0 figure, because €0 out of reach reads as an error rather than as good news.

Every value is a maximum or a count, so nothing here can be dragged down by matching a low payer.

Which pay number belongs at the top of Scores?

The shipped one is a median across the roles you match — which moves the WRONG WAY: match one more low-paying company and it drops, as if that were bad news.

The mix at the top is the recommendation; the four it was drawn from sit below it.

All of it uses today's real data. Only Amazon (8 roles) and Google (6) have scored roles at all, so every figure rests on two companies.

A — Best at each tier

Two maxima, one per tier. Cannot be dragged down by a low payer, and points straight at the action: convert the Possible, reach €95.2k.

Tradeoff: says nothing about how MANY roles sit at each tier.

B — Top-end access

Answers "am I locked out of the good money?" Low payers are simply not in the band being counted.

Tradeoff: the denominators are tiny while only two companies are scored — 1 of 6 is a thin claim.

C — Ceiling and what is locked

Both numbers are maxima, so nothing drags them down.

Tradeoff: degenerate today. The best-paid tracked role is already one you match, so it reads €0 out of reach and tells you nothing.

D — No pay band

Makes no aggregate claim, so nothing can be distorted. Counts lead; money stays on the rows where it is a fact about one role.

Tradeoff: no money picture at a glance.
This is the layout you picked and that is now live at /scores. The pay band inside it is what the other page is deciding about.
